en.title: The Book of Dao · Chapter Twenty-five · Undivided at Its Making
en.原文:
有物昆成
先天地生

蕭呵漻呵獨立而不𪻞
可以為天地母

吾未知其名
字之曰道
吾強為之名曰大

大曰筮
筮曰遠
遠曰反

道大
天大
地大
王亦大

國中有四大
而王居一焉

人法地
地法天
天法道
道法自然
en.字龕:
### 王 *wáng* — the king

**字 Graph** ｜ 篆 ![王之篆](/book-assets/hosuke-laozi-en/zhuan/%E7%8E%8B.svg)

**文 Gloss** ｜ The *Shuowen*: 「王，天下所歸往也。董仲舒曰：古之造文者，三畫而連其中謂之王。三者，天、地、人也，而參通之者，王也。孔子曰：一貫三為王。」 — "Where all-under-heaven comes home. Dong Zhongshu says: the ancient graph-makers drew three strokes and joined them through the middle — that is the king. The three are heaven, earth, and man; he who passes through and joins them is the king."

**像 Image** ｜ Three horizontals: heaven above, earth below, man between. One vertical passes through all three and joins them. The king is not the top stroke — he is the vertical: the human through whom above and below run together.

**義 Sense** ｜ "The king too is great" (王亦大 — so both silk manuscripts write, as does Wang Bi): the king's greatness is not a fourth heaven over the three — it is the capacity, in man, to join heaven and earth through the middle, made visible in one person. The king holds one place among the four greats because he is the joining, not the crown.

en.校記:
The text follows Manuscript A (MS A); the lines 蕭呵漻呵獨立而不𪻞, 大曰筮, 遠曰反 and 道大, and the last three lines, damaged in MS A, are supplied from Manuscript B (MS B). Graphs are those outside the brackets in the *Changsha Mawangdui Han mu jianbo jicheng* (2014; hereafter *Jicheng*).

- 有物昆成: The manuscripts agree; the *Jicheng* reads 昆 as 混 "undivided, merged". Wang Bi has 有物混成.
- 蕭呵漻呵獨立而不𪻞: Follows MS B. MS A reads 繡何繆何獨立□□□, with 何 read as 呵; the three graphs for "and does not change" are lost (end of MS A, col. 140). The *Jicheng* reads MS A's 繡 and 繆 and MS B's 蕭 and 漻 alike as 寂 "silent" and 寥 "empty". MS B's last graph is 𪻞 (王 beside 亥), read as 改 "to change"; Gao Ming's transcription gives 孩, but on the plate the left element is clearly 王. Wang Bi has 寂兮寥兮，獨立而不改, followed by a line, 周行而不殆, which neither silk manuscript has.
- 可以為天地母: The manuscripts agree; Wang Bi has 可以為天下母.
- 吾未知其名: Follows MS A; MS B reads 吾未知亓名也, ending in 也. Wang Bi has 吾不知其名.
- 吾強為之名曰大: The manuscripts agree; Wang Bi has 強為之名曰大, without 吾.
- 大曰筮: In MS A the repetition mark after 大 is lost and restored by the *Jicheng*; the line follows MS B. 筮 is read as 逝 "to pass on"; Wang Bi has 大曰逝.
- 筮曰遠 / 遠曰反: 筮曰遠 follows MS A. MS A's 遠 lay within a restoration in the 1980 edition and is read directly by the *Jicheng* from a small newly joined fragment; the repetition mark below it is lost and is treated as restored. 遠曰反 is lost in MS A and follows MS B, whose 反 is read as 返 "to return". (*Jicheng* IV, p. 52, n. 98)
- 道大: Lost in MS A; follows MS B. Wang Bi has 故道大.
- 王亦大 / 而王居一焉: Both manuscripts write 王 "the king", as the plates, the 1980 edition and Gao Ming's transcription all agree; transcriptions that give 人亦大 and 而人居一焉 are mistaken. Wang Bi has 王亦大 and 而王居其一焉.
- 國中有四大: The manuscripts agree; the *Jicheng* reads 國 "state" as 域 "realm". Wang Bi has 域中有四大.
- 地法天 / 天法道 / 道法自然: In MS A the repetition mark after 人法地 is lost and only 法天﹦法 survives; the rest is supplied from MS B, which links the clauses with repetition marks: 人法地﹦法天﹦法道﹦法自然.
en.疏:
杳眇曰：

此章言道之體用最為完整，學者不可不察。

夫帛書云「有物昆成」，王弼本作「有物混成」。昆者，渾淪之義，言道未剖之時，萬物一團而無間也。混則已涉於雜，昆則本然如是。有物昆成之義，所以明道先天地而生，渾然自存，非由湊泊。《大宗師》云「夫道有情有信，无為无形，自本自根，未有天地，自古以固存」，正此之謂。

次云「繡何繆何」（甲本，何讀為呵；乙本作「蕭呵漻呵」），王弼本作「寂兮寥兮」。寂寥者，虛無之狀；繡繆者，糾纏之貌，二義相異，然皆所以言道不可以形名求也。繡如絲之互織，繆如繩之相縈，道之於天下，無所不貫，無所不入，錯綜周流，其用廣矣。

「字之曰道，吾強為之名曰大」，此聖人不得已而立言也。道經首章云「道可道也，非恆道也」，強以字名，強以大稱，非妄作也。凡名皆假，讀者當得意忘言可也。

「大曰筮，筮曰遠，遠曰反」，王弼本以「逝」代「筮」，作「大曰逝，逝曰遠，遠曰反」。筮者，推演占度之義；逝者，往也，亦通。蓋道之為大，必有所往，往而後遠，遠而後返，周流不殆，終則有始。《易》曰「無平不陂，無往不復」，理在此矣。

王弼本作「域中有四大，而王居其一焉」；帛書作「國中有四大，而王居一焉」，義稍隘。域者無疆，國者有域，以道言之，域中為優。然四大之旨則一：道大，天大，地大，王亦大——帛書甲乙皆作「王」，與王弼本同。王者，人之代表也，人能參天地之大，唯以王為代表。

「人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然」，此四法之序也。人法地，取其厚德无私；地法天，取其覆載无私；天法道，取其不宰有功；道法自然，自然者非自然界，乃「自然而然」之自性——道之所以然者也。連道亦有所法，是自然者道之道也。此章之眼，於是乎在。

道之在天下，大矣遠矣，彌綸宇宙，而要歸自然。聖人知返，百姓日用而不知，學者苟會此循環之理，則道生天地之旨，思過半矣。
en.疏英:
Yaomiao says:

This chapter gives the most complete account of the Dao's substance and function in the whole book; a student must not skim it.

The silk text writes 有物昆成, "a thing undivided at its making," where the Wang Bi recension writes 混成. 昆 is undivided wholeness — the time before the Dao was cut open, when the ten thousand things were one lump with no seam. 混 already smacks of mixture; 昆 is simply what it is of itself. "Undivided at its making" shows the Dao born before heaven and earth, whole of itself, not pieced together from anything. The Great Ancestral Teacher says: "the Dao has feeling and faithfulness, no doing and no form; its own root, its own stock — before there was heaven and earth, from of old it stood firm." Just this.

Next, 繡何繆何 (so manuscript A, 何 read as 呵; B has 蕭呵漻呵), "woven, ah, wound round, ah," where Wang Bi has 寂兮寥兮, "silent, ah, empty, ah." Silent-and-empty is the look of vacant stillness; woven-and-wound is the look of threads interlaced — different faces, both saying the Dao cannot be sought by form or name. 繡 like silk woven through silk, 繆 like cord coiled on cord: through all-under-heaven the Dao runs, nowhere it does not reach, nothing it does not enter — interwoven, coursing round, its use is vast.

"I call it, by courtesy name, the Dao; forced to give it a name, I call it the Great" — the sage naming under protest. The book's first chapter says, "the Dao that can be spoken of is not the constant Dao": he forces the courtesy name, forces the name Great — and this is no arbitrary invention. Every name is borrowed; let the reader get the meaning and forget the words.

"The Great is called casting-forth (筮); casting-forth is called far; far is called turning-back." The Wang Bi text puts 逝 in place of 筮: "the Great is called passing; passing is called far; far is called turning-back." 筮 is the diviner's work — casting the yarrow, pushing the reckoning forth; 逝, passing, also passes as a reading. For the Dao to be Great it must go out; going out, it goes far; going far, it turns back — coursing round without fail, ending and so beginning. The Book of Changes: "no level that does not tilt; no going that does not return" — the law is here.

Wang Bi writes 域中有四大, "in the realm there are four greats," where the silk text writes 國中, "in the state." The realm is boundless; the state has borders — for the Dao's sake, the realm is the better. But the point of the four greats is one: the Dao is great, heaven is great, earth is great, and the king too is great — both silk manuscripts write 王, as Wang Bi does. The king is mankind's representative: that man can stand level with heaven-and-earth's greatness — only by the king as its representative.

"Man patterns on earth; earth patterns on heaven; heaven patterns on the Dao; the Dao patterns on the self-so" — the order of the four patternings. Man patterns on earth, taking its thick De that favors none; earth patterns on heaven, taking its covering-and-bearing that favors none; heaven patterns on the Dao, taking its accomplishing without ruling; and the Dao patterns on the self-so — not "nature" as the natural world, but the so-of-itself: that by which the Dao is what it is. Even the Dao has something it patterns on — the self-so is the Dao of the Dao. Here is the eye of the chapter.

The Dao in all-under-heaven: great, far, wrapping the cosmos — and coming home, always, to the self-so. The sage knows the turning-back; the hundred clans use it daily and never know. Let the student gather this law of the circle, and the point of the Dao's birthing heaven and earth is more than half understood.
en.英譯:
There is a thing, undivided at its making (有物昆成), born before heaven and earth.

Woven, ah, wound round, ah (繡何繆何 — so MS A; the text above follows MS B, 蕭呵漻呵, "still, ah, empty, ah") — it stands alone and does not change. It can be the mother of heaven and earth.

I do not know its name: I call it, by courtesy name, the Dao (字之曰道); and, forced to give it a name, I call it the Great (大).

The Great is called casting-forth (筮); casting-forth is called far; far is called turning-back (反).

The Dao is great; heaven is great; earth is great; and the king too is great.

In the state (國中) there are four greats — and the king holds one place among them.

Man patterns on earth; earth patterns on heaven; heaven patterns on the Dao; the Dao patterns on the self-so (道法自然).

校記:
本章帛書原文據甲本，「蕭呵漻呵獨立而不𪻞」「大曰筮」「遠曰反」「道大」及末三句甲本殘，據乙本補；字從《集成》（2014）括號外原字。

- 有物昆成：甲乙同，《集成》讀「昆」為「混」。王弼本作「有物混成」。
- 蕭呵漻呵獨立而不𪻞：從乙本。甲本作「繡何繆何獨立□□□」，「何」讀為「呵」，「而不改」三字殘（甲本第140行末）。甲之「繡」「繆」、乙之「蕭」「漻」，《集成》皆讀為「寂」「寥」。乙本末字作⿰王亥之「𪻞」，讀為「改」；高明實錄作「孩」，圖版左旁實作王。王弼本作「寂兮寥兮，獨立而不改」，下有「周行而不殆」一句，帛書二本皆無。
- 可以為天地母：甲乙同；王弼本作「可以為天下母」。
- 吾未知其名：從甲本；乙本作「吾未知亓名也」，句末有「也」字。王弼本作「吾不知其名」。
- 吾強為之名曰大：甲乙同；王弼本作「強為之名曰大」，無「吾」字。
- 大曰筮：甲本「大」下重文號殘去，《集成》補之，今據乙本。「筮」讀為「逝」，王弼本作「大曰逝」。
- 筮曰遠　遠曰反：「筮曰遠」從甲本；甲本「遠」字原在補文中，《集成》據新綴小殘片直接釋出，其下重文號已殘去，作補文處理。「遠曰反」甲本殘，據乙本，乙本「反」讀為「返」。（《集成》肆·頁52·注98）
- 道大：甲本殘，據乙本。王弼本作「故道大」。
- 王亦大　而王居一焉：甲乙原件皆作「王」，圖版、1980 釋文、高明實錄同；或錄作「人亦大」「而人居一焉」者，誤。王弼本作「王亦大」「而王居其一焉」。
- 國中有四大：甲乙同，《集成》讀「國」為「域」；王弼本作「域中有四大」。
- 地法天　天法道　道法自然：甲本「人法地」下重文號殘，唯存「法天﹦法」，餘殘，據乙本。乙本以重文號連讀，作「人法地﹦法天﹦法道﹦法自然」。
